title: probavi-manifest/1 and /2 — the backup manifest, a backup tool's statement about what it wrote
description: The backup manifest: one JSON file written beside a backup at backup time and named by target.source.manifest. Not docs/capabilities.json, which is the capabilities manifest. The core reads it before the sandbox is created and refuses the drill when the artifact disagrees. Normative document: ../../backup-manifest.md. Note that expected_checksum is computed under the rule in that document's §3 and is NOT the adapter-defined backup.checksum an evidence record carries: the two answer different questions and are not comparable (§4). Both published versions validate here, and a backup job chooses between them by what the core it drills with reads rather than by what this file accepts: probavi-manifest/2 is specified as of 2026-09-26 and no released core reads it yet (backup-manifest.md §11.1), so a manifest written today says probavi-manifest/1. An unknown schema value is a configuration error rather than a manifest to guess at, which is why adopting a version early fails a drill instead of degrading quietly.

schema.description: Pins the shape. Required; an absent or unknown value is a configuration error, not a manifest to guess at.

v2.title: probavi-manifest/2 — v1 plus an optional baseline

schema.description: Pins the shape. Required; an absent or unknown value is a configuration error, not a manifest to guess at.

baseline.description: What the backup job counted, per table, for the baseline check to reconcile against the restored database (backup-manifest.md §2.1). A key names a table the way the drill's engine names one, exactly as the table parameter does elsewhere: a collection, a label, a class or a key prefix where that is what the engine has. A value states an exact count or a range and nothing else, and a job that can state neither honestly omits the table. A key obeys the identifier rule a check's table parameter obeys, because the baseline check runs the adapter's declared statement against exactly that name. Never stands alone: a v2 manifest still states a checksum or a size, because refusing the drill before the restore is what this file is for. One constraint here is not expressible in JSON Schema and is enforced by the reader instead: rows_min must not exceed rows_max.

propertyNames.description: The same identifier rule a check's table parameter obeys (drill-config.md §3.5): at most two dot-separated segments, each starting with a letter or underscore. A name outside it is one the check could never run, so it is refused when the manifest is read rather than at the point the reconciliation would have failed.

rows.description: The exact number of rows the backup holds.

rows_min.description: The low end of the narrowest range the backup job can honestly state.

rows_max.description: The high end of the same range. Both bounds are required together; a one-sided bound is a tolerance wearing a range's clothes, and §2.1 declines to offer one.

expectedChecksum.description: The artifact's digest under backup-manifest.md §3, whose framing is stated to the byte there and reproduced by the shell recipe in §3.1: SHA-256 over a regular file's bytes, or the canonical tree hash for a directory. Not the adapter's backup.checksum.

expectedSizeBytes.description: A regular file's size, or the sum of every regular file's size in a directory.

createdAt.description: When the backup job says it produced the artifact. Informational: it is the backup tool's claim, and never populates the record's backup.created_at, which is the adapter's measurement of the artifact itself.

engineVersion.description: Informational. Version compatibility is enforced by the adapter, from the artifact, not from this file.
